title: A Production-Ready Cloud Deployment Checklist
content:
A release is ready when you can identify what will change, observe whether it works, and recover when it does not. A green build answers only part of that question. The production environment also includes credentials, networking, persistent data, background work, and the people who must respond if the change fails.

This checklist is an editorial release method for a small web service, not a universal compliance standard. Adapt it to the service's consequences and recovery needs. Google's release engineering chapter provides primary operational context for repeatable builds and controlled releases. The compact sequence here is deliberately smaller than a large organization's full delivery system.

Identify the actual release unit

Record the version or immutable artifact identifier, the source revision, and the configuration changes. Say whether the deployment replaces a container, uploads static files, migrates a database, or changes a proxy rule. A label such as “frontend update” is inadequate if the same operation also switches an API hostname or modifies authentication cookies.

Compare the intended target with what is actually running. Establish the service name, listener, upstream, and data location from current configuration. This is a local preparation recommendation: do not improvise discovery commands against systems you are not authorized to inspect. On shared infrastructure, unrelated services need clear boundaries before any restart.

Retain the previous artifact and configuration in a location the recovery operator can access. A Git revision alone may not reproduce a release if dependency downloads, build tools, or private registries have changed. Write down which artifact can be restored immediately and which would require a rebuild.

Prepare data and configuration separately

List persistent stores and any schema changes. Ask whether the old application can read the new schema and whether the new application can tolerate the old data during rollout. Prefer a staged compatibility plan when a change cannot be undone safely. Restoring an old application binary does not reverse a destructive data transformation.

Keep secrets out of the artifact and out of release notes. Verify that the intended runtime can obtain only the credentials it needs. Check configuration names and required values without printing secret contents into logs. A missing variable should cause a clear, controlled startup failure rather than quietly selecting a development service.

For a containerized service, inspect network publication explicitly. Docker's port-publishing documentation explains that publishing a port can expose it outside the host. A release review should therefore include the listening address and proxy path, rather than assuming that a healthy local response means the external boundary is correct.

Choose checks that represent the service

Test a read path, a permitted write path, an invalid input, and an unauthorized request where relevant. Include asset loading and redirects for browser applications. Use isolated fixtures when testing writes. Do not let a convenient smoke test create fake customer messages, send real email, or alter a production account without explicit authorization.

A health endpoint should have a stated meaning. Process liveness, dependency readiness, and successful completion of a user task are different observations. Google's monitoring chapter discusses signals such as latency, traffic, errors, and saturation. Select a small relevant set and establish the current baseline before interpreting a change.

Define stopping conditions in advance. Examples might include a failed sign-in path, repeated application errors, or a mismatch between expected and observed data. These are suggested categories, not universal numerical thresholds. The service owner should choose limits using actual traffic and consequences, not numbers copied from another team's dashboard.

A hypothetical form-service deployment

Imagine a hypothetical team releasing a new contact form API. The candidate passes validation tests, but the release also changes its database connection setting. The preparation note names both changes, retains the prior image, and confirms that the schema remains readable by the previous version.

The team uses a local fixture to check valid submission, missing email, and duplicate retry behavior. Their post-release plan checks the public form, API error signals, and queue processing using an authorized test method. If the API accepts requests but the worker cannot process them, the release is not considered healthy merely because the homepage loads.

The restoration plan distinguishes returning to the old application from restoring the database. The former can be appropriate for a code regression. The latter would discard new submissions unless they are preserved and reconciled. Writing this distinction beforehand prevents an apparently quick rollback from becoming a data-loss incident.

Handoff checklist

  • Name the release artifact and previous recoverable version.
  • Record every configuration and schema change.
  • Confirm the exact service, network path, and data store.
  • Keep credentials out of logs and release documentation.
  • Explain what health checks prove and what they omit.
  • Use authorized, isolated smoke-test inputs.
  • Assign an observer and a person empowered to stop.
  • Write the restore procedure and its data consequences.
  • Check the real user journey after activation.
  • Retain evidence and rollback material until the review window closes.

Scale the checklist to the release, but keep its claims precise. “Candidate validated” is different from “production activated,” and “endpoint responded” is different from “customer workflow completed.” A useful release note names the strongest result actually observed and leaves unresolved checks visible to the next operator.
excerpt: Prepare a cloud release with artifact identity, data compatibility, meaningful health checks, explicit stop conditions, and a recovery plan that protects new data.
